title: Describing someone
topic: describing looks and personality; ser, tener, llevar
why: After possessives and the family, this lesson gives you the tools to describe a person: ser for looks and personality, tener for hair and eyes, llevar for clothes. It recycles adjective agreement and the ser / estar contrast, and sets up the lesson on likes.

¿Cómo es? Looks and personality with ser

To describe what someone is like, Spanish uses ser: it's their identity, what doesn't change from one day to the next. The question is ¿Cómo es? (What's he like? What does she look like?). Don't confuse it with ¿Cómo está?, which asks how someone is doing. English uses “to be” for both; Spanish makes you choose.

¿Cómo es tu hermano? — Es alto, moreno y muy simpático.What's your brother like? — He's tall, dark-haired and really nice.

Looks

SpanishEnglish
alto / altatall
bajo / bajashort (height)
delgado / delgadaslim, thin
moreno / morenadark-haired, dark-skinned
rubio / rubiablond / blonde
pelirrojo / pelirrojared-haired, redhead
guapo / guapagood-looking, handsome, pretty
joven (jóvenes)young
mayor (mayores)older, elderly (polite)

Personality

SpanishEnglish
simpático / simpáticanice, friendly (not “sympathetic”!)
antipático / antipáticaunfriendly, unpleasant
tímido / tímidashy
divertido / divertidafunny, fun
serio / seriaserious
trabajador / trabajadorahardworking
hablador / habladoratalkative, chatty
amablekind, nice
alegrecheerful, upbeat

As you've seen, Spanish adjectives agree in gender and number, while English ones never change: mis primas son simpáticas. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant don't change in the feminine (amable, joven), except those in -or: trabajador → trabajadora.

For an older person, the polite way to put it is Es mayor. To soften a flaw, add un poco: Es un poco tímido. Muy makes it stronger: Es muy divertida. Joven takes an accent in the plural: jóvenes.

Tener and llevar: hair, eyes, clothes

Tener: what you naturally have

As in English, you “have” long hair or blue eyes, but Spanish adds the definite article: Tiene el pelo largo. Tiene los ojos azules. Note that el pelo is singular, just like English “hair.”

SpanishEnglish
tener el pelo largo / cortoto have long / short hair
tener el pelo rizado / lisoto have curly / straight hair
tener el pelo blancoto have white hair
tener los ojos azules / verdes / marronesto have blue / green / brown eyes
tener barba / bigoteto have a beard / a mustache

For a beard or a mustache, Spanish uses no article, where English says “a”: Mi padre tiene barba (my dad has a beard).

Llevar: what you're wearing

Llevar is a regular -ar verb that means “to wear”: clothes, glasses, a bag. It's the verb you use to describe what someone has on today.

Hoy Marta lleva una camiseta blanca y unos vaqueros.Today Marta is wearing a white T-shirt and jeans.
Mi abuela lleva gafas.My grandmother wears glasses.

Colors are adjectives, so they agree, and they come after the noun. Azul, verde and marrón only change in the plural (azules, verdes, marrones); rojo, blanco, negro, amarillo have four forms: una chaqueta negra, unos zapatos negros.

Las gafas is always plural, like English “glasses”: Lleva gafas. And marrón loses its accent in the plural: los ojos marrones.

", "

Parecerse a: who do you look like?

“To look like, to resemble” is parecerse a, a reflexive verb. Its first person is irregular, like conozco: me parezco. Learn it as it is; the other forms are regular. And don't forget the little preposition after it, which English “look like” doesn't need.

Personparecerse
yome parezco
túte pareces
él, ella, ustedse parece
nosotros, nosotrasnos parecemos
vosotros, vosotrasos parecéis
ellos, ellas, ustedesse parecen
Me parezco a mi madre: tengo sus ojos y su pelo.I look like my mother: I have her eyes and her hair.
Mi hermana y yo no nos parecemos nada.My sister and I don't look alike at all.

A full description

A good description strings the three verbs together: ser for the person, tener for features, llevar for clothes.

Mi primo Álvaro es alto y delgado. Tiene el pelo corto y barba. Siempre lleva gafas. Es muy trabajador, pero un poco serio.My cousin Álvaro is tall and slim. He has short hair and a beard. He always wears glasses. He's very hardworking, but a bit serious.

A common trap for English speakers: “he's dark-haired” is not said with tener on its own. You say Es moreno (he's dark-haired) or Tiene el pelo moreno (he has dark hair), but never “tiene moreno.” And moreno can also mean “tanned”: in summer, estoy muy moreno, with estar since it's temporary.
